articles.title_orig: Report: Trump did nothing with intel that China planted spy close to Nvidia CEO
articles.title_zh: Report: Trump did nothing with intel that China planted spy close to Nvidia CEO
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump apparently is so aligned with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—who has become the president’s key advisor on AI —that he ignored intelligence indicating that Huang was the target of a “Chinese spy plot,” and did so partly to protect Nvidia’s stock.
The New York Times spoke with people briefed on US intelligence agencies’ surveillance and granted them anonymity to discuss findings drawn from “classified intelligence.” According to sources, about a year ago, Trump was briefed that “Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access” to Huang. That “someone” was Alice Huang, or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen and former top executive at a Singapore cloud company called Megaspeed.
According to sources, the US had already suspected that Alice Huang—who is not related to Jensen Huang—was helping China evade export controls to gain access to high-end Nvidia chips through Megaspeed. But it alarmed investigators to discover that she may have used her role at Megaspeed to gain direct access to Jensen Huang. It’s now believed she may have leveraged that closeness to feed China intel not only on one of America’s leading AI companies, but also to influence Trump’s thinking on AI. As Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent noted last month ahead of Trump’s AI talks with China President Xi Jinping, “the president is completely aligned with Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia.”
At least partly due to fears that US action against the alleged spying could hobble Nvidia chip sales or disrupt the delicate US-China trade truce, Trump “chose not to do anything with the information,” sources said.
Soon after US scrutiny increased, Alice Huang’s name was removed from Megaspeed corporate documents. At this stage, it’s unclear “how closely she is still connected to Megaspeed,” NYT reported.
Liu Chang, the spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington, DC, told NYT that the US accusations against Alice Huang are baseless. He accused the US of pursuing a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against China.
It’s not clear which agencies were investigating Alice Huang or what triggered their suspicions, NYT reported. Sources also could not explain what information she may have shared with Beijing.
Nvidia has denied that she would have had access to any trade secrets, but it seems notable that Jensen Huang did not receive a defensive briefing that Americans sometimes get when they’re targets of foreign spying. Some senior officials think it’s unlikely that Jensen Huang would have “remained unaware” of Alice Huang’s alleged intelligence-gathering for the entire duration of their professional relationship, although Trump was told Jensen Huang had no knowledge at the time of his briefing. It seems possible that Jensen Huang got no briefing because US agencies worried that he might tip her off that “she was being watched,” the NYT reported.
Trump’s deep ties with tech leaders have been criticized throughout his administration, but Jensen Huang’s influence increasingly stands out . To critics, the political friendship appears to be largely based on growing his business in China. Since cozying up to Trump, the Nvidia CEO has gotten export controls relaxed and even struck a controversial deal giving the US a 25 percent cut of some chip sales so he could try to sell more chips in China. Sources told NYT that “some investigations and proposed trade sanctions involving China or Nvidia” have “ground to a halt within the Commerce Department” due to Jensen Huang’s influence.
No one’s sure when Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, but NYT found social media photos that predated her role arranging a Megaspeed purchase of $2 billion in chips over the next year. If those chips ended up in China, the US worried they “could help adversaries like China develop new weapons, surveil dissidents, and leap ahead of the United States in AI development,” NYT reported. To US agencies, it’s particularly concerning that Megaspeed may be doing China’s bidding by supplying chips to giant data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia “that appear to remotely serve customers in China,” NYT reported earlier this month.
Sources told the NYT that US intelligence agencies conducted electronic surveillance of Alice Huang and found that “she was in contact with an American citizen.” Since agencies could not legally surveil the American citizen without a court order, they sought to unmask the citizen by showing a “need for information.”
“In this case, the unmasking process identified Mr. Huang as the US citizen,” NYT reported.
Megaspeed is an Nvidia customer, and Nvidia has independently investigated whether Megaspeed is funneling its chips to China. That investigation concluded that there were no signs of diversion and that Megaspeed has raised no red flags as a customer, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told NYT.
Both Nvidia and Megaspeed insist that the cloud company has Singapore-based owners, but NYT visited the supposed offices and talked to anyone they could find to probe the actual business operations. Among red flags raised, NYT noted that staffers suggested “it’s not clear” what Megaspeed as a company does and confirmed that the Singapore director, James Tan, lives in China and is “never present.” (NYT’s review of corporate ownership documents showed Tan owns the shell company that owns Megaspeed.)
In that story published earlier this month, NYT detailed how Alice Huang was seemingly growing increasingly close to Jensen Huang, citing several photos of them together. That includes a photo at an event where she reportedly bragged, “I bet you guys I can get Jensen here,” and then he arrived in his trademark leather jacket to take whiskey shots.
Rizzo said that it was common for Nvidia’s CEO to attend parties with customers and partners, where he discussed “updates on the market.” One source told NYT that Jensen Huang had always planned to attend that party.
“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected,” Rizzo said. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”
However, the US government has been investigating Megaspeed since 2024, and they’ve found suspicious boxes of Nvidia equipment that seem to be ready to ship out, rather than installed. Earlier this year, the Department of Justice took over the Commerce Department’s investigation, and Megaspeed remains under scrutiny even though Nvidia’s probes uncovered no evidence the company was helping China dodge export curb violations.
Aaron Bartnick, an assistant director for technology security and governance under the Biden administration, told NYT that Megaspeed raised “many red flags.” Among them are the company’s “ownership claims and possible ties to sanctioned entities, that should have made Nvidia’s executives question whether they should have permitted the company to have access to its AI chips.”
“It’s hard to see a justification for taking that risk,” Bartnick said.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Sinks 350 Points; Google Stock's Tumble in Focus — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Sinks 350 Points; Google Stock's Tumble in Focus — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Google parent company Alphabet sank Thursday by more than 12%, in its worst one-day performance ever, wiping out more than $500 billion in market value.
Alphabet is America’s fourth-largest company, worth a total of $3.42 trillion, as of midday. Still, the amount of value it shed Thursday ranks as the second-worst wipeout in market history, only behind Nvidia’s $589 billion drop in 2025 .
The sharp drop in its stock price Thursday was the latest sign of broader anxiety across Wall Street over how long it will take big artificial intelligence companies to see consistent returns on  investments worth hundreds of billions of dollars.
On Wednesday, Alphabet reported its latest quarterly financial results , revealing that revenues fell short of Wall Street’s expectations.
It also reported lackluster advertising sales.
The “magnitude” of the slowdown in Google’s search business was “steeper than expected,” JPMorgan Chase analysts wrote in a Thursday morning note.
A senior Alphabet executive told investors Wednesday that part of the reason ad revenues from search were underperforming was because of Google’s own “AI Mode” search feature, which was resulting in fewer ads.
The company is working on addressing this, senior vice president Philipp Schindler said on the investor call, adding that “ad experiments” in the feature have “shown promising results.”
Company executives tried to soften the blow for investors by touting more than 1 billion users of its Gemini AI app.
But all that AI is coming at a massive cost to Alphabet, which disclosed that it has committed to more than $1 trillion worth of multiyear spending agreements to fund the infrastructure, energy and leases required to run AI systems.
The company said during its July earnings report that it planned to spend more than $200 billion this year, which is double what it spent in 2025. The company in June also raised almost $80 billion in capital, also to spend on the ever-expanding AI build-out.
Alphabet’s disappointing results also came against the backdrop of better results from its peer Microsoft , whose shares initially rose in after-hours trading Wednesday and overnight before reversing course to fall about 1.5% by 1:20 p.m. ET Thursday.
The big drop in Alphabet shares dragged down the Nasdaq Composite index, which was down 1.5% by the afternoon. The S&P 500 fell slightly less, by about 0.4%.
Shares of chip companies that supply equipment for AI data centers followed Alphabet shares lower, with the Philadelphia semiconductor index dropping 1.6%.
The bleeding even spread beyond the tech sector, as shares of construction equipment giant Caterpillar — a key supplier of the machines required to build data centers — plunged 9% early Thursday.
Caterpillar’s recent earnings report revealed that the company’s revenues beat Wall Street expectations but by less than many traders had hoped.
The industrial giant was the second worst performing stock on Thursday in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, behind only Alphabet. The Dow declined slightly more than 200 points.
As investors clamor for ever-higher returns from companies linked to the costly AI build-out, stock in firms that only narrowly top earnings targets, like Caterpillar, has been punished with dramatic sell-offs.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's relationship with China just got even more complicated as report says Jensen Huang was target of spy plot
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's relationship with China just got even more complicated as report says Jensen Huang was target of spy plot
articles.content_orig:
An Nvidia spokesperson on Thursday pushed back on a New York Times report that detailed American intelligence agencies surveilling a person close to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang because they thought she could be a Chinese intelligence asset.
According to the Times report , which cited people briefed on intelligence surveillance, Alice Huang, who is linked to the Singapore-based cloud Megaspeed, developed a close relationship with Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
Intelligence agencies worried that she was a spy, helping the Chinese government gain information from Nvidia and Jensen Huang, and fretted that Nvidia's CEO had access to President Donald Trump.
The Nvidia spokesperson pushed back on the story in a statement to CNBC, saying that Singapore-based Megaspeed is another one of the company's regional cloud customers, and that Jensen Huang's interactions with its officials are not unusual, because he speaks with thousands of customers every year.
The spokesperson added that customers don't get access to Nvidia trade secrets or relevant national security information.
The report also alleged that Megaspeed was previously suspected of helping companies evade U.S. export controls on Nvidia's AI chips, which aren't allowed to be shipped to China.
Nvidia said that Megaspeed had already been investigated for evading export controls.
"The diversion allegations against this regional cloud were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year," the spokesperson said in a statement.
Nvidia implied that the U.S. government had not briefed Nvidia on Alice Huang.
"We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know," the spokesperson said.
Nvidia has had to walk a tightrope in Washington as its AI chips have become a powerful tool for all AI developers and a bargaining chip in economic competition with China.
Politicians and analysts say that Nvidia's AI chips could be used to create Chinese military AI models, or commercial AI models that could compete and eventually surpass American technology.
As AI has become more important to the government, Nvidia's Huang has befriended Trump and has given pro-American speeches about building U.S. AI infrastructure.
Huang has appeared with Trump at state dinners, AI summits, and international trips, all while pushing for certain Nvidia chips to get a green light to be shipped to China.
Earlier this year the U.S. government cleared Nvidia's H200 chip to be shipped to China, but Chinese regulators prevented their imports. H200s are Nvidia's Hopper generation chip, not the current faster Blackwell generation currently used by American AI developers.
The Nvidia spokesperson said the Chinese government is not looking for Nvidia products from regional clouds like Megaspeed.
"Instead, the PRC government blocked U.S. AI chips, protecting its own industry and resulting in the largest write-offs in U.S. tech history," the Nvidia spokesperson said. Last year, Nvidia wrote off about $4.5 billion in Chinese-tuned AI chips.

articles.title_orig: 'Operation Supercharge': Japan and U.S. agree to develop Japanese missile facility
articles.title_zh: 'Operation Supercharge': Japan and U.S. agree to develop Japanese missile facility
articles.content_orig:
From left, Philippines Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro, Australia Defense Minister Richard Marles, Japan Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and U.S.Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth prepare to leave after posing for pictures before holding a Quadrilateral Meeting on the sidelines of the 20th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defence Ministers' Meeting (ADMM) and 13th ADMM-Plus Meetings in Cebu, Philippines, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Rolex Dela Pena/Pool EPA via AP hide caption
CEBU, Philippines — The United States and Japan have agreed to establish a Japanese facility for the joint production of advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles, the Japanese defense chief said.
It is the latest move by the allies, which have repeatedly expressed alarm over China's growing assertiveness in Asia.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi made the announcement in a news conference Wednesday night in the central Philippine province of Cebu, where he met U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of an annual meeting of Southeast Asian defense chiefs and their major Asian and Western counterparts.
Koizumi raised concern Thursday about China's increasing naval activity in southwestern Japan. He said that three Chinese destroyers and a coast guard ship together crossed the Osumi Strait south of the southern main island of Kyushu and headed east to the Pacific Ocean this week. It was the first such fleet configuration his ministry has spotted, he said.
Koizumi said he cited the incident as "an example illustrating the challenging security environment in the region" in his remark at a session Thursday. His ministry will keep watching the Chinese activity with high level of interest, he said. Japan has been accelerating military buildup in southwestern Japan to deter China.
The annual meetings aim to avert a major regional conflict and strengthen defense cooperation. On the sidelines of the meetings, however, the U.S. and China and their allies have often traded criticisms.
The missiles that will be produced as part of a joint effort called "Operation Supercharge" are essential for the F-35 fighter jets, Koizumi said. The two sides agreed to build a final assembly and inspection plant for the Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM, in Japan, he said. The U.S.-made F-35s are one of the world's most advanced aircraft and are also used by the Japanese military.
During his brief meeting with Hegseth in Cebu, Koizumi said he "shared a sense of crisis … regarding the increasingly severe regional situation and we agreed to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. alliance with greater speed and intensity than ever before."
"We reaffirmed the importance of a free and open international order based on the rule of law, which rejects any attempts to unilaterally alter the status quo through the use of force, coercion or other means," Koizumi said.
Hegseth renewed the Trump administration's repeated assurances of commitment to help deter aggression in the region in a separate meeting on Wednesday with ASEAN defense ministers, who were led by the host, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. Like Koizumi, Hegseth did not mention China by name in expressing his security concerns in the region.
"The approach we're taking, we describe as strong, quiet and clear," Hegseth told the ASEAN defense chiefs. "Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics to let our actions speak for themselves."
His message is "clear enough that our friends, our partners and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners," Hegseth said.
Hegseth has assured the Philippines, the oldest treaty ally of Washington in Asia, that the Trump administration will build a robust deterrence against China's increasingly aggressive actions in the disputed South China Sea. Beijing claims the busy waterway, a key global trade route, virtually in its entirety.
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles said his country's forces, along with allies like the U.S., will press on with efforts to defend the rule of law despite China's increasing assertiveness, including in the South China Sea. Australia protested last year after a Chinese J-16 fighter aircraft released flares and passed within 30 meters (100 feet) of an Australian P-8 Poseidon surveillance jet over the disputed waters.
"That doesn't deter us from doing what we need to do and that's essentially asserting the rules-based order here in the end of the Pacific," Marles told The Associated Press in Cebu on Wednesday. "Freedom of navigation on the high seas is profoundly important for Australia."
The Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei, all ASEAN member states, along with Taiwan, also have overlapping claims in the South China Sea. Confrontations have particularly escalated between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and navy vessels in disputed shoals and outlying waters.
Washington has warned that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces, ships and aircraft come under an armed attack, including in the South China Sea.
Beijing and Tokyo have a separate dispute over tiny Japanese-controlled islands in the East China Sea, with both sides often accusing the other of infringing on their maritime territory.

articles.title_orig: China's Communist Party seeks to tighten discipline
articles.title_zh: China's Communist Party seeks to tighten discipline
articles.content_orig:
Chinese President Xi Jinping, center left and Zhang Shengmin, Vice Chairman of the Central Military Commission second from right attend a ceremony in honor of fallen national heroes at the Monument to the People's Heroes to mark Martyrs' Day at Tiananmen Square in Beijing, Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Ng Han Guan/AP hide caption
BANGKOK — China's top leaders on Thursday elevated the only remaining general on the commission that oversees the country's military to the Politburo, the top governing body of the Communist Party.
The leaders also adopted a resolution on strengthening self-governance, discipline and anti-corruption in the party, as they seek to extend their grip on power.
During a four-day closed-door meeting, top Communist Party leaders deliberated on and adopted resolutions that will guide the party in the coming years. The meeting comes about a year before President Xi Jinping is widely expected to secure his fourth five-year term as the party's leader.
The party elected Gen. Zhang Shengmin, who currently serves as vice chairman of the Central Military Commission, to the Politburo. Xi had earlier purged two of China's top generals, leaving Zhang as the commission's only member besides Xi himself. It also left the Politburo without any representatives from the People's Liberation Army.
Zhang also holds a position overseeing internal discipline for the military, serving as deputy secretary of the CMC Commission for Discipline Inspection.
The party said in a summary of the resolution that the tasks facing it were "increasingly arduous," such as "uniting and leading the people to safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests."
It said it must step up its self-governance, which involves rooting out corruption and maintaining ideological purity.
The party should, "with an eye on enhancing its long-term governance capacity, maintain its progressive nature and purity, and its close, flesh-and-blood ties with the people," according to a summary of the resolution from the official Xinhua News Agency.
Xi has championed anti-corruption since coming to power in 2012, and has sustained a crackdown on officials for more than a decade. However, analysts say the focus now also includes underperforming officials.
Party members also reviewed the earlier purges of top members and military officials, confirming the personnel changes.
The plenum meeting revealed wider-than-expected purges, according to analysis by Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at Asia Policy who studies Chinese politics. He calculated an attendance rate of 74 percent, the lowest since the times of former leader Mao Zedong, who ran political purges regularly.

articles.title_zh: The average 30-year US mortgage rate dips to 7.24%, the lowest level in more than a month
articles.content_orig:
The current U.S. job market has been described as a "low-hire, low-fire" environment — relatively stable, even as unemployment edges up and wage growth stagnates . But there is another kind of low being expressed by workers — their level of engagement.
Gallup's quarterly polling of the workforce on engagement — which tracks workers’ focus, motivation and enthusiasm for their jobs — fell to its lowest level since 2011 in the third quarter of 2026.
The decline was concentrated in remote and hybrid employees across the U.S., according to Gallup, particularly "those in organizations that have adopted artificial intelligence."
The quarterly data does need to be put into the longer-term context for a poll that Gallup has conducted since 2000. Back in 2000, its inaugural polling found 26% of U.S. employees were engaged, and the data moved in a relatively tight band, between 26% and 30%, through 2013. The all-time peak of 36% occurred during the Covid year of 2020.
But the most recent data is notable nonetheless. The 29% mark that employee engagement fell to in Q3 2026 was two percentage points lower quarter over quarter, breaking below a floor that had been set through the first half of the year. After the Covid year peak, engagement has been on the decline, dipping to 31% by 2024, but then remaining at that level through the first half of 2026. It's not an all-time low, but it has erased most of the gains from the years leading up to the Covid record.
And according to Gallup's approach, the survey results represent a significant number of workers, with each percentage point representing about 1.6 million U.S. employees, or roughly 3.2 million fewer engaged workers quarter over quarter in Q3.
Gallup polled a random sample of 21,648 adults, aged 18 and older, from Aug. 5-19, 2026, with the poll's margin of sampling error plus or minus 1 percentage point at a 95% confidence level. The results for remote and hybrid workers exceeded the margin of error.
Among all workers, morale has been on the decline, according to the poll. In Q3, 46% of those polled said they strongly agreed they knew what was expected of them, down from 49% in the first half of the year. Thirty-seven percent said they strongly agreed that their supervisor or someone at work cared, down from 40% in the first half of the year and well below the Covid peak of 47% in March 2020. In 2025, these two measures had already registered the largest five-year declines in Gallup's polling.
Gallup says the data is important in terms of its link to many core business goals: productivity, customer service, quality, safety and profitability, while "those who are not engaged or are actively disengaged are psychologically disconnected from their work and employer."
In Q3 2026, "actively disengaged" employees represented 18%, while 53% of all employees were "not engaged."
The polling organization's recent research has found that worker concerns about expectations in their roles declined roughly twice as much among hybrid and fully remote employees. "The Q3 findings add to concerns about how well organizations communicate expectations and maintain employee connections across different work arrangements," Jim Harter, chief scientist for Gallup's workplace management and wellbeing practices, wrote in a survey analysis.
"Since 2020, hybrid and fully remote employees have experienced larger declines in clarity of expectations than on-site employees in remote-capable jobs. These findings raise the possibility that physical distance can contribute to psychological distance between employees and their organizations, particularly as companies navigate the use of AI at work," Harter wrote.
Gallup pointed to a sharp narrowing in engagement among remote and hybrid employees at organizations that have adopted AI as a factor to monitor. In Q3, what it refers to as the "engagement advantage" associated with employees at AI integrated organizations had narrowed from five points among remote employees and eight points among hybrid employees to two points and three points, respectively, across the cohorts.
One quarter of data cannot indicate whether a new downward trend in the national workforce has begun. And Gallup's data cannot show AI to be the specific cause of any decline in employee sentiment. In addition, other recent reads on the U.S. workforce present a mixed picture.
The Conference Board's annual Job Satisfaction Index , released in June, rose to 68.9%, the highest level recorded in its 39-year history, though it noted the gains were concentrated in "higher-income workers, men, and workers confident in AI's impact on their careers."
The American Psychological Association's annual workplace survey , conducted between May and June, found year-over-year declines among workers asked if their workplace was "healthy" and whether they felt valued on the job, while reports of tension and stress on the job increased in 2026.
ADP Research's Employee Motivation and Commitment Index increased in October for the second consecutive month, but it remains well below where it was a year ago, and has been mostly on the decline since August 2025.
To be sure, these surveys are not asking exactly what Gallup asks. And with employee engagement at its lowest level in 15 years, hybrid and remote employees leading the way down, and all employees showing signs of insecurity on the job, Gallup's Harter concluded that the pattern suggests, among other things "that AI adoption may be outpacing the communication and managerial support needed to make it effective."

articles.title_orig: Robust consumer spending, AI-related investment power US economy in third quarter
articles.title_zh: Robust consumer spending, AI-related investment power US economy in third quarter
articles.content_orig:

Driven by strong consumer spending and a surge in artificial intelligence investments, the U.S. economy expanded at a healthy 3.4% annualized pace between July and September, accelerating from the second quarter.
Figures released Thursday by the Commerce Department show that third-quarter gross domestic product—measuring total output across goods and services—outpaced the 2.2% growth recorded from April through June. Household spending increased at a swift 3.8% rate while business investment climbed sharply amid the boom in AI technology.
The performance demonstrates the ongoing resilience of the world’s largest economy, despite higher energy costs brought on by fighting with Iran. Growth surpassed expectations, topping the 3% expansion projected by forecasters in a survey by data firm FactSet.
Commercial investment, excluding housing, rose 12.7% as growth was lifted by AI spending. Capital outlays on information processing equipment jumped 37.4%, software rose 9.6%, and research and development increased 7.5%. Conversely, residential investment, constrained by high mortgage rates, fell 3.3%, marking its sixth decline in the last seven quarters.
Thursday’s report represents the first of three Commerce Department estimates regarding third-quarter GDP growth.
Inflation data was also released on Thursday. An inflation gauge closely monitored by the Federal Reserve accelerated last month, showing that prices remain elevated less than a week before midterm elections in which affordability concerns have become a central issue.
Consumer prices rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier, the Commerce Department said Thursday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices climbed 0.5%, up from 0.3% in August and the highest figure since May.
Annual inflation has worsened since the Iran war caused spikes in oil and gas prices. U.S. oil prices still top $100 a barrel, up from less than $70 before the war. Polls show that the rise in inflation has soured most voters on the economy and President Donald Trump's handling of rising costs. Trump campaigned in 2024 on lowering prices, including bringing the cost of gas below $2 a gallon. It currently averages about $4.25 a gallon nationwide.
Excluding the volatile energy and food categories, inflation also picked up. It increased 3.1% from a year ago in September, up from 3% in August. And from August to September, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the previous month.
The reports come a day after the Federal Reserve, the agency tasked with combatting inflation, left its key interest rate unchanged. With inflation above the Fed's 2% target and the economy charging ahead, the central bank will remain under pressure to raise rates at its next meeting in December.
Thursday's inflation data comes from the personal consumption expenditures price index, which typically echoes the better-known consumer price index published earlier this month. The Fed more closely monitors the PCE index because it puts less weight on housing prices and allows for changes in consumers' shopping habits.

articles.title_orig: At least 14 people killed in Russian attack on Dnipro train station
articles.title_zh: At least 14 people killed in Russian attack on Dnipro train station
articles.content_orig:
The site of the drone strike has been sealed off, as Ukrainian authorities continue their investigation
At least 14 people have been killed after a Russian jet-powered drone hit a crowded platform at the main railway station in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, local officials have said.
Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said at least 14 others were wounded in the attack, including an 11-year-old boy.
Ukraine's state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, said a passenger train headed for the southern city of Zaporizhzhia was at one of the platforms in Dnipro when the drone hit.
Russia's military has not publicly commented. It has repeatedly hit Ukraine's large railway network, but Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians.
In Dnipro, an elevated threat level was announced ahead of Thursday's strike, according to the railway operator chief, Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
"But unfortunately there were still a large number of people on the platform" when the drone struck, he said.
Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov said the incident was a tragedy, adding that a drone hit an electric civilian train.
Pictures from the Ukrainian rescue services show a large hole in a platform that is strewn with blurred-out bodies, near a blast-damaged train with smashed windows.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said "the Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."
He called for further US, European and G7 sanctions on Russia and repeated his criticism of a controversial deal that was struck earlier this month between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, which eased some sanctions on Moscow, allowing the US to import Russian diesel.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, two girls aged 15 were killed in a Russian missile attack on the centre of Chernihiv city, in the north of the country, regional head Vyacheslav Chaus said. At least 25 others, including four children, were injured, he added.
A day of mourning has been declared for Chernihiv and Dnipro on Friday.
In the city of Kremenchuk, in the central Poltava region, three people were killed and 28 injured in a Russian drone attack that hit residential buildings and a school, regional head Vitaliy Diakivnych said.
At least 25 people were injured in the Russian strike on Kremenchuk, local officials said
The latest Russian strikes came during efforts to uphold a fragile ceasefire in the besieged city of Oleshky, which has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and where residents have been trapped without food, water, medicine and electricity for years.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, wrote on Telegram that the truce was holding into a third day.
Meanwhile, the Kremlin has condemned Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow whilst the city hosts the Russia-Africa Summit, the Tass news agency has reported. The two-day event is attended by African leaders and government delegations from 48 countries.
The mayor of Moscow said 613 Ukrainian drones were launched overnight towards the region, most of which were shot down during their flight.
Russia's defence ministry has always denied targeting Ukrainian civilians and says its attacks on railways target the infrastructure used to transport military personnel and equipment.
However, the dangers to passengers are very real, and attacks on Ukraine's train infrastructure have risen sharply.
Of the 521 locomotives hit since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, almost 60% have been hit this year, according to statistics released by Ukrzaliznytsia supplied to AFP news agency.
Overall attacks on railway facilities have risen from 1,206 in 2025 to 1,700 so far this year.
There appears to have been a wider assault on Ukraine's infrastructure in recent weeks, with two bridges attacked in the capital Kyiv, and a metro train hit during one of the strikes.

articles.title_orig: U.S. economy grew at a fast clip this summer, thanks to business, consumer spending
articles.title_zh: U.S. economy grew at a fast clip this summer, thanks to business, consumer spending
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. economy grew 3.4% in the July to September quarter from a year earlier, a much faster pace of annual growth than in the second quarter. Consumer spending was one of the main drivers of growth — though many Americans continue to struggle with inflation. Joe Raedle/Getty Images North America hide caption
The U.S. economy grew faster in the summer compared to the spring, driven by consumer spending as well as investments in AI.
Gross domestic product, which broadly measures economic activity, grew at an annual rate of 3.4% July through September, according to a report from the Commerce Department released Thursday. The previous quarter GDP grew at a 2.2% annual pace.
A big driver for GDP growth in the third quarter was the strong investments from AI companies, which continue to build out data centers and spend big money in developing the technology.
Meanwhile, consumer spending was another of the big drivers of GDP growth, led in part by higher-income Americans who are better able to withstand stubbornly high inflation.
The sturdy GDP data comes just days before the midterm elections, with many Americans saying they feel gloomy about the economy as inflation jacks up the costs of many day-to-day necessities, while the ongoing conflict with Iran drives up energy costs like gasoline.
Although consumer spending has been growing steadily, it has not spread out evenly across households, with lower-income Americans struggling more than high-earners. Wage growth has also fallen behind inflation, further squeezing many Americans.
Siri Steven, a manager at a resale store in Decorah, Iowa, says she and her husband are putting off fixing up their more than 130-year-old house.
"We barely go out to eat now," Steven said. "I really have to be mindful of our budget and make sure that we can pay all our bills and not overdraft."
She also says her family hasn't been able to save, going paycheck to paycheck. The personal saving rate for the U.S. in September is 3.8%, according to a separate report from the Commerce Department, down from 4.1% in August.
Prices rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier, according to the same report, faster than the Federal Reserve's 2% target. The Fed watches the Commerce Department's inflation measure closely, particularly when deciding what to do with its benchmark interest rates.
Still, the central bank decided against raising rates Wednesday, with added pressure to raise rates during the next meeting in December after Thursday's reading on prices.
Economists also are concerned about the country's long term fiscal health. Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, warns that despite solid GDP figures, economic growth feels delicate. That's due to business and consumers having to navigate around Trump Administration policies, such as tariffs and the U.S. war against Iran.
"We're growing," Zandi said. "The economy is moving forward but it's a very, very fragile growth. It doesn't feel like we're kicking it in on all cylinders."

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq falls as Alphabet set for record loss amid AI spending woes
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq falls as Alphabet set for record loss amid AI spending woes
articles.content_orig:
Alphabet shares were down sharply following the opening bell on Thursday while Microsoft traded largely flat as investors focused on the tech giants' latest spending and free cash flow numbers in their third-quarter earnings.
Alphabet plummeted 12% in morning trading while Microsoft was little changed.
If Alphabet closes more than 9.77% lower on Thursday, it would be its worst post-earnings reaction ever. The company went public in 2004.
Microsoft reported $45.2 billion in capital expenditures and finance leases during the third quarter, which was 30% higher than a year ago, but below analyst projections of $50.67 billion. Free cash flow fell 27% to $18.63 billion but remained positive.
Alphabet, in contrast, reported negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion for the third quarter, which fell much further than the $2.70 billion analysts expected by analysts. The Google parent maintained its full year capital expenditure guidance of between $195 billion and $205 billion.
The earnings report comes as investors scrutinize AI spending plans of tech companies and are focusing on the returns on those investments.
"Microsoft is building out its architecture in a measured way and as such contains fewer surprises," Ben Barringer, global head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said on Thursday.
"Alphabet, by contrast, saw its share price hit after hours as a result of a fairly messy set of results and a poorly handled earnings call," Barringer added.
Alphabet's biggest source of revenue, search advertising, grew 12% in the September quarter to $63.35 billion, but missed analyst expectations, adding further pressure to the company's shares.
Philipp Schindler, Alphabet's chief business officer, said the impact on the search business was partly because of lower monetization within the company's AI Mode. He added that Alphabet is now "scaling" ads within its AI Overviews and AI Mode products, including in international markets.
Google's search business has faced headwinds from the rise of other AI chatbots like OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude. People may be carrying out more search queries outside Google. Gemini, Google's own AI chatbot, has failed to keep pace.
"The problem for Google is it faces an innovator's dilemma and doesn't know whether to protect its core business or look to join the disruption. As such, Google has lost its edge with Gemini and is behind peers on agentic AI," Barringer said.
Google's dominant market share in the search business, however, could ultimately give it a leg up over its peers, Rosenblatt Securities analyst Scott Devitt said.
"I don't think it's a sea change," Devitt told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Thursday. "If it's a problem for Alphabet, it's a problem for any consumer-facing AI agent or LLM as well. And so, it's a problem that I think is ultimately going to be resolved. And when it does, Alphabet, with its 4 billion search customers that become AI customers, is in an enviable position."
- CNBC's Robert Hum, Samantha Subin, Jordan Novet and Caleigh Keating contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: China leaders demand more loyalty and more initiative
articles.title_zh: China leaders demand more loyalty and more initiative
articles.content_orig:
The top echelon of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) held a four-day session behind closed doors in Beijing this week, with the talks focusing on strict leadership and discipline inside the ruling party.
Xi Jinping , who is both the CCP's general secretary and the head of state in China , signaled he would not only deepen the existing anti-corruption effort , but also ensure that party officials demonstrate more loyalty and more initiative at all levels.
According to the press release published on Thursday, the committee published a resolution praising the leadership and Xi Jinping for "enormous political courage and strong sense of responsibility" in tackling the issues of corruption and the weakening of the Party's governance.
The statement emphasized the need to "consistently advance comprehensive and strict Party leadership."
Kerry Brown, head of the Lau China Institute at King's College London, says Xi wants to minimize potential sources of instability.
Amid the current international tensions and the internal problems in China, including economic difficulties, Xi is pursuing his anti-corruption campaign and by demanding loyalty . "This is just going to intensify because if [the CCP] isn't disciplined and united, the party believes that it will go the same way as everywhere else in the world at the moment and become disunited and unstable," Brown told DW.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Xi also recently spoke of the necessity to identify and remove "two-faced functionaries" from the political system.
In his speech, which was published in mid-October by the party's Qiushi Magazine, Xi referred to people professing loyalty to the central leadership while working against its instructions and following their own "individualistic" goals. The Chinese president described them as "political opportunists." He also criticized party officials pretending to be "nice guys," as in, those who use harmony as an excuse to stand aside when problems arise.
Brown points out that China's political system is now facing a crucial dilemma: If officials at all levels are now indeed expected to show innovation and courage in solving problems, the party's control could grow weak. This could, in turn, boost corruption.
However, if CCP leaders lean more on the "strict Party leadership" aspect and ramp up the pressure on the rank-and-file, there is also the danger of suppressing initiative. This could go beyond the party itself and could even affect the military.
The party is "very, very risk averse," Brown points out.
Chong Ja Ian, a political scientist at the National University of Singapore , notes that party functionaries under Xi only have a limited space to make their own decisions.
Taking this into account, the party's push for individuals to show initiative is not necessarily a major issue.
"I believe Xi would like for the officials to act proactively and decisively by conducting specific tasks; but he still doesn't want them thinking for themselves so much that they can question the agenda he prescribed. The 'proactivity' demanded by Xi is limited to the implementation, not decision-making," he told DW.
Brown adds that Xi seems to be ready to sacrifice a certain amount of operational flexibility to gain more control and stability.
"As long as you have unity, you live for another day, right? But if you have disunity, you probably die the same day," he told DW.
This approach "kind of works," at least at the moment, he added.
"It's not like the Chinese economy is disastrous. It's not great, but it's not disastrous. In any case, look at the outside world. It's a mess."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Outside observers are also focusing on Xi's future and possible successors for the 73-year-old leader .
For now, Xi seems to be firmly in control. It is highly likely that he would be confirmed as the party's general secretary next fall, and could stay in that position until 2032.
This is due to the changes pushed by Xi in 2018 , which removed term limits for state and party leaders.
Both analysts told DW that the issue of succession plays a major role in Xi's push towards internal stability.
"There's always a danger of differences in the party fragmenting it, especially when the question of succession comes up," says Brown. "And even though we don't expect to see a successor anytime soon, you know, there's going to be speculation about who might succeed Xi."
"He can't go on forever," he added.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Political scientist Chong Ja Ian says that Xi currently holds all the power. Therefore, the CCP leader could be afraid of his authority being undermined if he named a successor ahead of time.
"On the other hand, a failure to make preparations on time could create a power vacuum that can cause major instability," he told DW. "To solve this dilemma, the current leader needs to have both the necessary self-confidence and the readiness to take a step back — just like his predecessors did. But not everyone has that kind of confidence."
This text was originally published in Chinese.

articles.title_orig: Google admits AI search makes less money, but it’s fixing that with more ads
articles.title_zh: Google admits AI search makes less money, but it’s fixing that with more ads
articles.content_orig:
Google parent Alphabet reported its Q3 financial results on Wednesday afternoon, showing a healthy rise in revenue for the months of July to September. But the company’s stock price has taken a beating, marking one of the largest post-earnings drops in its history. It comes down to several troubling aspects of the new report, including an admission by the company that AI search isn’t earning as much as organic search, and despite that, Google expects to spend even more on AI next year.
The company took in almost $128 billion in Q3 2026, earning more than $26 billion in net income. These may sound like good numbers, but financial markets are not impressed. While revenue is up 25 percent versus last year, net income is almost $9 billion lower. As of this story’s publication, the stock price is down almost 12 percent, and it was down about 13 percent earlier in the day.
While revenue was up 25 percent year over year, analysts expected more. Google reported earnings per share of $2.12, but the consensus projection ahead of Wednesday was $3.02. Google’s Cloud products actually beat expectations, crossing $30 billion in revenue. That’s about a billion more than analyst guesses.
Google is still making a huge amount of money, but there are several troubling trends emerging. The last few years at the company have been all about AI, with generative technology appearing in products from Gmail to Android. Most notably, Google is shifting to an AI search platform powered by Gemini models.
During the earnings call, Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler discussed the company’s search volume. This is one of the key metrics by which Google tracks its own performance. In the last quarter, Google saw search grow by 12 percent versus last year. Good for the company, right? Except that’s a much slower rate than previous quarters. Growth in Q2 was 17 percent, and Q1 saw 19 percent growth over 2025. Search revenue was also flat in Q3.
So that’s the first problem, likely driven by more consumers using AI chatbots to find answers. The other issue is that Google’s take on AI search isn’t pulling in revenue like standard web search yet. According to Schindler, each AI Mode query earns less revenue compared to a similar web search—there are fewer ads, and they cost less to run.
While Schindler suggested AI mode revenue was set to increase, he was also careful to control expectations. Advertisers may need time, he said, to understand the value in AI search ads. The company’s research reportedly shows that users find these ads more relevant and helpful than the ones they see in traditional search.
As part of the financial disclosure, Google announced an expansion of ads in AI Mode. If you do decide to dip into Google’s search chatbot, you’ll probably see more contextual advertising. These ads will begin appearing in more international markets soon. In the US, where AI Mode ads were already becoming commonplace, Google will implement multi-turn ads. That means the sponsored links will change continuously as you engage in a back-and-forth with the robot. CEO Sundar Pichai noted that these complex interactions are becoming more common as Google pushes more users toward AI Mode.
Google is not slowing down—it’s only going to accelerate the shift toward more AI. Like last quarter , Google reported negative cash flow in Q3. The loss actually increased from -$5.8 billion to -$9.06 billion, a situation that is directly attributable to Google’s runaway AI spending. Google had capital expenditures of $51.4 billion in Q3 and says it still expects total 2026 spending to be between $195 billion and $205 billion. In 2027, Google is targeting more than $300 billion of AI investment.
Credit:
                                      Google Credit:

          
          Google
To support this continued spending, Google points to its cloud revenue more than doubling over the past year. It’s easy to see why the company is so keen to keep expanding in AI based on that. The company’s AI compute infrastructure doesn’t just power Gemini. Countless AI startups pay to run models on Google’s infrastructure. But even the larger AI firms are using venture cash to do it, and if that funding were to dry up, Google’s cloud revenues could go with it.
While Google’s investments ensure it still turns a profit, the trend of spending more than it earns on products and services (that negative cash flow) could come back to bite it. Search growth is declining, and Google is placing all its eggs in the AI basket. If spending on cloud services in the industry drops or search growth stalls, the company could be looking at a lot more red in its future.

articles.title_orig: China's PIPL at 5: Enforcement, evolution and what comes next
articles.title_zh: China's PIPL at 5: Enforcement, evolution and what comes next
articles.content_orig:
CIPP/E, CIPP/US, CIPM, FIP
Senior information governance officer
Beyond Change Advisory, Hong Kong China Network Security Association
In 2023, the fifth anniversary of the EU General Data Protection Regulation's implementation led to widespread reflection on its effectiveness, faults and international influence. The international cascade of regulations that followed the GDPR's introduction bolstered the idea of the Brussels effect, the phenomenon through which regulation within the European market influences global standards.
One of the most prominent examples is China's Personal Information Protection Law , which shares many of the GDPR's fundamental concepts. Effective 1 Nov. 2021, the PIPL now celebrates its fifth anniversary.
Comparable concepts include their respective principles, definitions of personal data and information and the roles and obligations of data handlers, the PIPL's equivalent to the GDPR's "controllers."
While these comparable approaches may make it easier for organizations to harmonize their operations, the two laws are not like-for-like. Among the most notable deviations is the Chinese approach to lawful bases. The PIPL does not contain an equivalent to Europe's "legitimate interests" basis, with consent relied upon far more heavily.
Now that the PIPL has had time to develop, the law's fifth anniversary provides its own opportunity for reflection on guidance and enforcement under the law to date.
Enforcement mainly comes under the remit of the Cyberspace Administration of China, though other authorities also contribute, primarily the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and Ministry of Public Security and certain sectoral regulators.
While landmark cases are handled by the CAC, enforcement actions involving mobile apps are often addressed by different authorities. Civil litigation has also emerged as a means for challenging unlawful processing, with multiple "guiding cases" now identified, providing greater clarity on specific PIPL compliance requirements.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Tankers strike mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says, as Hegseth fires top general
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Tankers strike mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says, as Hegseth fires top general
articles.content_orig:
Iran has not yet responded to a letter sent by Vice President JD Vance to the secretary of the Iranian Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, according to the semi-official Tasnim News agency, which is closely affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Tasnim said in a Thursday post on its official Telegram social media account that Tehran was not prepared to drop any of its core conditions for a ceasefire, which include lifting the American blockade of Iran's ports, easing sanctions and giving Iran access to its frozen financial assets held abroad, among other things.
Multiple news outlets have reported that Vance's letter to Rezaei was an attempt to restart peace negotiations, but President Trump said Wednesday that it was a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Iran's navy said a tanker it described as violating maritime restrictions was damaged and caught fire after striking sea mines east of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving the vessel unable to continue sailing.
In a statement, the navy said the incident occurred before noon on Thursday as the tanker was sailing through an area designated as prohibited and unsafe by Iran
The U.S. has encouraged shippers to use a shipping route in the south of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has insisted vessels can only use northern routes it has authorized.
The navy's statement warned that the Strait of Hormuz was closed "to violating vessels that, without coordination and relying on the lies of the U.S. president, intend to pass through prohibited and unsafe areas."
"These uncoordinated transits through high-risk areas have exposed and will continue to expose vessels and their crews to serious dangers," it added.
Qatar has categorically denied allegations of interfering in Israel's elections or funding efforts to influence their outcome, accusing Israeli politicians and media figures of launching a disinformation campaign to drag the small Persian Gulf state into domestic Israeli political disputes.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Majid al-Ansari said in a statement that Qatar would not be used as a scapegoat for Israeli politicians' failures, insisting that Doha had no involvement in Israel's political competition and would continue its mediation efforts between Iran and the U.S., as well as wider diplomatic engagement and support for the Palestinian people.
His comments come after Israeli President Benjamin Netanyahu alleged that Tuesday's national elections were "stolen by Arab parties" and claimed foreign interference in the vote.
Israel's Shin Bet internal security service is investigating possible Qatari and Turkish funding used in an effort to influence the election outcome, according to reports by the Jerusalem Post and Israel's Channel 13.
"These accusations are ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure," al-Ansari said. "The repeated invocation of Qatar in Israeli electoral rhetoric reveals an excessive obsession with our country among certain Israeli political and media figures."
Iran's navy has carried out more than 20 operations against U.S. warships and approximately 300 operations targeting American interests in various locations during the war, Iranian Army Navy Coordinating Deputy Rear Admiral Jalil Moghadam said in an interview published Thursday by the official state-run news agency IRNA .
Moghadam claimed the operations involved missiles and drones and said Iran's navy remains operational despite repeated claims by President Trump and other U.S. officials saying it has been destroyed.
"If the Iranian Navy has been destroyed, why have these forces not come closer than 500 or 600 kilometers to the Strait of Hormuz, or closer than 300 kilometers to our maritime borders? There is a force standing in their way, and that force must be the Navy," he said.
Moghadam did not offer any evidence to substantiate his claims.

"Prove your claim of mine-clearing in the Strait of Hormuz with independent evidence, not a statement!" demanded Mohebi in a post on X , adding that "the reality of the Strait of Hormuz is determined in the skies, on land and at sea — not on social media or in America's  media-warfare rooms."
Earlier Thursday the IRGC said three oil tankers had been disabled after striking mines in the strait, and the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center confirmed one vessel in the area was seen on fire.
In late August, President Trump and CENTCOM chief Adm. Brad Cooper insisted the primary shipping lanes of the Strait of Hormuz had been demined and were safe for commercial vessels.
In a statement posted online, Cooper said the U.S. military had "meticulously and quietly" cleared mines previously laid by the IRGC.
"Internationally recognized transit routes in the strait are free of Iranian sea mines thanks to the incredible work of the U.S. military," he said. "Today, international shipping lanes are open, and momentum is building."

"As an initial toll, 12 citizens were killed and three others were critically injured when the Saudi enemy targeted the homes of the families of Ibrahim Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz and Al-Raabi Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz in Al-Barah, Maqbana district," the Houthi health ministry said in a statement shared by the group's Saba news agency.
Following an uneasy four-year truce, fighting reignited in Yemen in July, months into the U.S.-Iran conflict that has plunged the wider region into crisis. The Saudis, who back Yemen's government, have engaged in fighting with the Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coast and in deadly back-and-forth strikes.

The secret network of military agencies has helped Iran usher at least $2 billion in components into the country since 2025, evading Western sanctions and, since earlier this year, the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and vessels.
Some of the agencies are linked to Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), others to business conglomerates run by the country's elite, Reuters said.

The hardware was brought in from China, Russia and Germany, Reuters reported.
The agencies all use the address of Iran's Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics in Tehran. Most were established in 2013, when Iran was struggling under international sanctions, the investigation found.

In a statement, the provincial intelligence directorate said the operations were carried out in recent days following public tips and ongoing intelligence and operational surveillance, in cooperation with other provincial security forces. articles.title_orig: Germany does not seek decoupling from China, wants fair trade, president says during Beijing visit
articles.title_zh: Germany does not seek decoupling from China, wants fair trade, president says during Beijing visit
articles.content_orig:
Germany does not seek to decouple from China but wants to address trade imbalances through dialogue, the German president said Thursday.
"Our goal as Europeans is clear. We do not want to decouple from China," Frank-Walter Steinmeier told an audience at Peking University during his visit to Beijing.
"On the contrary, we want to ensure that trade continues to be of benefit to both sides ... Partnership only holds if both sides have something to gain. That is why we are seeking solutions through dialogue for the sectors where great imbalances have arisen," Steinmeier said.
Competition between German and Chinese companies is beneficial "but only when it is based on fair rules and a level playing field," he said.
Steinmeier said Germans do not want the world to split into blocs or see a new confrontation between them, warning that such divisions could undermine international security and cause economic losses.
"It is understandable that China wants to protect its economy against external shocks and negative influences. However, China having greater autonomy must not mean conversely that others are increasingly dependent on China and vulnerable to it," he said.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Wednesday that Europe does not seek a trade war with China but is determined to defend its industries from unfair practices.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has said the EU’s trade deficit with China in 2025 reached €1 billion ($1.12 billion) per day.
The market share of three major German automakers declined in both Europe and China since 2021, while the added value that these manufacturers generated in Europe dropped by 30-45% in the first half of this year compared to 2021-2022.

The United States and Japan have agreed to establish a production facility in Japan to jointly manufacture advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles , according to the Japanese defense chief.
The decision marks the latest step by the two allies to bolster security capabilities amid heightened concerns over China 's growing military assertiveness across Asia.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi announced the agreement during a news conference Wednesday evening in Cebu, a province in the central Philippines .
His remarks followed a bilateral meeting with U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of an annual gathering of Southeast Asian defense chiefs and their major Asian and Western counterparts.
During a session on Thursday, Koizumi highlighted increased Chinese naval presence near southwestern Japan, noting that three Chinese destroyers alongside a coast guard vessel recently passed through the Osumi Strait south of Kyushu into the Pacific Ocean.
He stated that it was the first time his ministry had recorded such a fleet configuration.
Koizumi pointed to the transit as "an example illustrating the challenging security environment in the region," adding that Tokyo will maintain close surveillance of Chinese naval operations while continuing to accelerate its own military buildup in southwestern Japan.
The annual meetings aim to prevent major conflict and deepen regional cooperation, though the U.S., China, and their respective allies frequently exchange criticisms during the proceedings.
The joint manufacturing effort, titled "Operation Supercharge," will establish a final assembly and inspection plant in Japan for the Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM.
Koizumi emphasized that these missiles are essential for F-35 stealth fighters, which are operated by both the U.S. and Japanese militaries.
Recounting his meeting with Hegseth, Koizumi said he "shared a sense of crisis … regarding the increasingly severe regional situation and we agreed to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. alliance with greater speed and intensity than ever before."
He added: "We reaffirmed the importance of a free and open international order based on the rule of law, which rejects any attempts to unilaterally alter the status quo through the use of force, coercion or other means."
In a separate meeting with ASEAN defense ministers led by Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr., Hegseth offered renewed assurances regarding Washington's commitment to regional stability.
Without calling out Beijing by name, Hegseth outlined the U.S. approach.
"The approach we’re taking, we describe as strong, quiet and clear," Hegseth told the defense chiefs, adding it is "Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics to let our actions speak for themselves."
He emphasized that the position is "clear enough that our friends, our partners and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners."
Hegseth reassured the Philippines, Washington’s oldest treaty partner in Asia, that the Trump administration will maintain robust deterrence against Beijing’s actions in the South China Sea, a critical trade waterway claimed almost entirely by China.
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles pledged that Australian forces, alongside allies like the U.S., would continue upholding international law despite Chinese actions in disputed waters.
Referring to an incident last year where a Chinese J-16 jet released flares near an Australian P-8 Poseidon surveillance plane, Marles said: "That doesn’t deter us from doing what we need to do and that’s essentially asserting the rules-based order here in the end of the Pacific."
He added: "Freedom of navigation on the high seas is profoundly important for Australia."
Territorial claims in the South China Sea remain contested among the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, and Taiwan, with frequent standoffs involving Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval vessels.
Washington maintains that it is bound by treaty to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces, ships, or aircraft come under armed attack. Separately, Tokyo and Beijing remain locked in a maritime dispute over Japanese-controlled islands in the East China Sea.

articles.title_orig: A rock formation collapse in Turkey’s touristic Cappadocia region kills at least 3
articles.title_zh: A rock formation collapse in Turkey’s touristic Cappadocia region kills at least 3
articles.content_orig:
Parts of a large volcanic rock formation crashed down in Turkey’s popular tourism destination of Cappadocia on Thursday, killing at least three people and injuring five others, officials said.
A section of the rock formation — known as a fairy chimney — tumbled in Cappadocia’s Goreme region, prompting authorities to deploy medical and rescue teams.
Gov. Huseyin Kok said recent heavy rains likely caused the collapse, which occurred near a parking lot at an entrance to the site.
He said rescue teams were continuing to search for other people who may be trapped under the debris.
“We hope that there are no other casualties,” the governor said. “We are deeply saddened.”
Kok said two of the three dead were Turkish nationals. He did not provide information on the third victim.
Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation was launched into the incident.
HaberTurk news channel showed heavy machinery removing chunks of rock from the foot of the formation.
Cappadocia, in central Turkey, is a UNESCO World Heritage-listed site famed for its distinctive rock formations and ancient underground cities. It is one of the country’s most visited tourism locations.
The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day holiday, when the area would have been crowded with visitors.

Here are the main headlines from and about Germany on Thursday, October 29, 2026:
A German news magazine's decision to publish private interview notes has sparked a controversy surrounding Berlin's potential next mayor.
On Thursday, Der Spiegel published internal comments on an interview by Elif Eralp, who led the socialist Left Party (Die Linke) to victory in September's state election. Her office had accidentally included the remarks while approving an interview for publication.
In the notes, Eralp expressed fears for her family's safety if she publicly named Ibrahim Ibrahim, a pro-Palestinian activist who is reported to have links to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), which the EU designates a terrorist organization. Ibrahim had attended the Left Party's election-night celebrations and was photographed with prominent Left Party Bundestag member Ferat Koçak.
Eralp also cited advice she received from Berlin police against publicly naming individuals linked to organized crime, though that advice was reportedly related to a separate case. Der Spiegel questioned whether her fears could affect her independence as mayor. Eralp rejected suggestions that she could be intimidated and pledged firm action against terrorism and organized crime.
She is reportedly considering legal action against the magazine and a complaint to Germany's Press Council. The magazine has also faced criticism for publishing remarks intended for internal use, raising questions about the balance between public interest, privacy, and journalistic ethics.
The timing is significant. Eralp, the daughter of Turkish immigrants, could become Berlin's first Left Party mayor and the first woman of Turkish descent to hold the office. Her party won 25.7% of the vote in September's election and hopes to form a government with the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens. Both prospective partners have approved formal coalition negotiations.
The Left must decide whether to follow suit at a party conference this Saturday, October 31. The far-left party is also facing accusations of antisemitism involving some of its members. Newly elected lawmaker Vanessa Emde faces possible exclusion from the Left's parliamentary group following comments questioning whether states, including Israel, have an inherent right to exist. The Left has been part of Berlin coalition governments before but has never led one. The controversy comes at a pivotal moment in its effort to do so.
Germany 's leaders are on a foreign relations push, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz on a trip to South Korea , German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul in Panama and German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier in China .
Merz spoke of the threat North Korea posed to Europe's freedom by supplying troops to fight in Russia's invasion of Ukraine. He wraps up his visit with a trip to the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on Friday.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, meanwhile, is in Panama where he is visiting ahead of traveling to Atlanta for the G20 meeting.
Wadephul is there to promote free trade and also handed over humanitarian supplies to his Panamanian counterpart Javier Martinez-Acha Vasquez.
And then German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier ditched the formalities in China and picked up a ping-pong paddle for a game with Germany’s most famous table tennis player, Tino Boll, who is accompanying Steinmeier as a special guest on his state visit.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul landed in Panama on Wednesday evening for a visit.
After his arrival at Panama City airport, Wadephul handed over humanitarian supplies to his Panamanian counterpart Javier Martinez-Acha Vasquez.
The aid shipment is made up of about 20 tons of supplies. Panama was hit by a powerful earthquake earlier this month .
The supplies include water filters, blankets, tarpaulins, cots and kitchen sets worth over €150,000 ($167,000).
More than 5,000 people are still being housed in emergency shelters, weeks after the magnitude-7.7 quake on October 9, which resulted in injuries and damaged hundreds of buildings.
Wadephul also thanked the Central American country for maintaining the Panama Canal "so responsibly and ensuring it is fit for the future, as well as more generally focusing on preserving balance in the region."
Restrictions on other sea routes due to the conflict in the Middle East has meant that the Panama Canal is more important to global trade than ever.
Wadephul is due to hold talks on Thursday with Martinez-Acha Vasquez and President Jose Raul Mulino.
Wadephul will travel to the US state of Georgia for the G20 summit in Atlanta on Friday and Saturday.
Several names are being floated to replace Frank-Walter Steinmeier as Germany's ceremonial head of state — including some that could be the first woman to hold the post.

After delivering his speech at Peking University, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier ditched the formalities to play ping-pong with Germany’s most famous table tennis player, Tino Boll.
In the university sports hall, the two faced each other, accompanied by two Chinese participants — a referee and the university president. Right from the start, Steinmeier downplayed his chances, and subsequently lost 1–7.
Boll, who won silver at the Beijing Olympics in 2008, is the most successful German table tennis player of all time.
He won several Olympic medals, as well as titles in World Cups and World Championships during his storied career, which saw him ranked as the number 1 player in the world in 2003, 2011 and 2018.
To this day, Boll remains one of the best-known Germans in China, where ping-pong is unofficially considered the national sport.
Boll is accompanying Steinmeier as a special guest on his state visit.
Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on Thursday called on China to reduce economic imbalances between the two countries, as well as between China and Europe.
Steinmeier, who was speaking at the renowned Peking University, also urged China to work with Germany and other European nations to strengthen the international, rules-based order and "to advocate for peace and free global trade."
The German president, who holds a largely ceremonial role, spoke of his respect for China's rapid development in its economy, technology and politics, calling China a "defining world power."
But Steinmeier added, "With greatness and power comes great responsibility."
"We are not concerned about China's rise. We are watching how China rises," he said.
"We do not want to decouple from China; on the contrary, we want to structure trade in such a way that it continues to benefit both sides." This, he said, requires fair and uniform rules.
Steinmeier was referring to the high barriers European companies face when trying to operate in the Chinese market. Since China heavily subsidizes its exports to Europe, the European market comes under pressure too quickly.
This poses "the danger of one-sided vulnerability," Steinmeier said. Europeans cannot want this for their economy, just as "China does not want it for its economy."
He also called on China to exert more influence on Russia to bring the war in Ukraine to an end.
According to Steinmeier, China's interests are also at stake in this war, just as they are in the Middle East. As a major trading power, China also needs free sea lanes, intact supply chains, and a secure energy supply.
"The longer these conflicts persist, the weaker the global economy as a whole becomes — and with it, one of its largest economies: China," the president said.
Steinmeier addressed future issues in which China should take a particular interest: climate change and artificial intelligence. He appealed to his hosts, saying that when it comes to AI, "we should jointly establish international guidelines so that the technology remains under human control," he said.

articles.title_zh: DoorDash stock pops, Instacart falls after companies announce $17 billion acquisition deal
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
DoorDash ( DASH ) announced plans to acquire hyperlocal grocery delivery provider Instacart ( CART ) on Thursday morning in a deal valued at $17 billion.
DoorDash, which is primarily known for its restaurant food delivery business, will pay $65 per Instacart share, a 26% premium over the stock's Oct. 22 closing price. The transaction includes 75% cash, with Instacart stockholders able to elect cash, DoorDash stock, or a combination of both. Instacart's board of directors unanimously approved the deal, according to a press release.
"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online," DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in the release. "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery."
DoorDash stock popped over 5%, while Instacart stock fell 1.5%.
The acquisition comes as Walmart ( WMT ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) have been taking share of the grocery delivery market, especially for same-day and one-hour delivery.
Prior to the announcement, Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian said the combination of Instacart and DoorDash could "potentially prove to be a competitive differentiation."
"A combination of strong restaurant delivery plus a marketplace including various grocers from Instacart can be a critical combination against Walmart and Amazon in particular, who continue to push in this market as well," Arounian said.
Walmart currently holds a roughly 30.9% share of the online grocery market, ahead of Amazon at roughly 23.6%, per Wedbush.
For customers worried about what the Instacart acquisition means for prices, the company said shoppers will now get two memberships for the price of one and more choices.
"Instacart customers could shop at more than 50,000 additional stores, on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today," the release said.
For local business owners, the company said this would allow them more ways to earn.
